title: Tenali Raman and the Three Noble Suitors
summary: A wealthy and cultured nobleman of the court, Lord Somasundaram, had an accomplished, intelligent daughter named Madhavi. Three eligible young noblemen sought her hand in marria...
keywords: the tale of the three suitors
full_text:
A wealthy and cultured nobleman of the court, Lord Somasundaram, had an accomplished, intelligent daughter named Madhavi.
Three eligible young noblemen sought her hand in marriage:
Prince Jayadeva, a handsome warrior;
Lord Haridasa, a wealthy merchant;
And Master Ananda, a modest scholar and musician.

Unable to choose among them without causing factional discord, the nobleman appealed to King Krishnadevaraya, who referred the matter to Tenali Raman.

Tenali arranged a private trial in the palace garden pavilion.
Lady Madhavi sat behind a translucent silk screen that completely obscured her facial features, allowing only her voice and silhouette to be perceived.

Tenali called the three suitors into the garden one by one.
To Prince Jayadeva, Tenali said:
'Describe the maiden behind the screen, and tell us why you desire to marry her.'
Jayadeva puffed out his chest: 'She must possess the radiance of the morning sun! I will dress her in gold armor, conquer kingdoms for her glory, and she shall be admired by all men as the most beautiful queen of my palace!'

Next came Lord Haridasa, the merchant. He said:
'Her father is wealthy and connected to the spice guilds. I will shower her with pearls, diamonds from Golconda, and seven palaces of marble. Her beauty will be the crowning jewel of my commercial empire!'

Finally came Master Ananda, the scholar.
He sat upon the grass, looked at the quiet silhouette behind the screen, and spoke softly:
'I do not know whether her face is fair as the lotus or humble as the field flower. But I have heard her speak of compassion for the sick; I have heard her verses honoring truth; and I have heard the music of her gentle kindness.
I seek to marry not a trophy of glory or an ornament of wealth, but a kindred soul with whom to share life’s sorrows and joys, reading books, cultivating a garden, and walking together in mutual reverence.'

Behind the silk screen, Lady Madhavi wept tears of profound joy.
Tenali smiled and turned to Lord Somasundaram:
'The first man loves his own pride; the second loves his own gold; but the third loves your daughter’s soul. A marriage of pride crumbles in defeat, a marriage of gold shatters in poverty, but a marriage of true hearts endures through all seasons.'

Lady Madhavi was wed to Master Ananda, living in deep harmony and love, celebrated as a union blessed by true wisdom.
moral: True love perceives the inner character and spirit of a person, while superficial passion sees only outward form.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Tale of the Three Suitors"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
